items.title: Name Shame
items.author: Ernie Smith
items.content:
The concept of nominative antideterminism, or when your name goes against everything that you represent, whether intentionally or not. Cecil Fielder, sadly, wasn't a great fielder.

If I lived my life in a nominatively deterministic way, I would be a Muppet blacksmith. But unfortunately, I live in the real world, and my lot in life has put me on newsletter-writing duty. So I don’t quite live up to my name. But lots of other folks don’t, either. Recently, though, I had a bit of a thought monster: What about people or things whose lives have more or less completely gone against what their names suggest they should? I’ve seen a couple of names for this, but I’m going with nominative antideterminism, the idea that not everyone needs to live up to the lot in life they’ve been given on the surface. And the guy that got me thinking about it? A famous baseball player who definitely did not live up to his last name—and his son arguably didn’t, either. Today’s Tedium ponders the oddness of nominative antideterminism, which I guess lazy people could just call “irony.”

The estimated number of people in the U.S. with the last name “Smith,” well above the second-most-common last name, Johnson. That number is significantly more than the number of blacksmiths in the U.S., a number that is around 5,000 to 10,000 based on various historic estimates. Sorry to tell you this, in case you have yet to figure it out on your own: Not everyone named Smith is a blacksmith.

Cecil Fielder doing what he does best: Hitting a home run.

A designated-hitter dynasty: Were the Fielders good fielders?

that the best baseball player I knew of was great at hitting home runs … and not much else.

His name is Cecil Fielder, and he was basically the first player in more than a decade to hit 50 home runs in a single season, a mark that eventually opened the floodgates for years of home-run races (and yes, doping scandals). Fielder’s performance for the Detroit Tigers during the early 1990s was frequently in conversation for the AL MVP, getting close but never quite clinching it. Problem was, the Detroit Tigers weren’t a particularly good team back then, even if Fielder himself was an electric player.

But Cecil Fielder, who was notably a fairly big guy for a baseball star, had a problem, and it’s one that is laid out cleanly on his Wikipedia page:

Fielder also had a reputation as a below-average fielder, mostly caused by his poor speed and range.

This, my friends, is a great example of nominative antideterminism. Often, we draw attention to people whose name more of less lived up to their lives.

See that smile on his face? That’s the look of a man who never thought he would steal a base.

But Fielder, who was always a better slugger than a runner (he infamously only stole two bases in his entire 13-year career), did not excel at the very thing his name suggested he would. This most assuredly explains why he was regularly used as a designated hitter.

A surprising number of “Prince Fielder error” videos on YouTube, but to be fair, most of us would probably not love our errors getting shared with the world. Just ask a journalist whoo doezn’t kno how 2 spel.

His also-successful son, Prince Fielder, had a somewhat better reputation as a fielder than Cecil did. But he also led the league in errors at his position more than once, hinting that he might have also only partly lived up to his name.

Defensively, he recorded a .992 fielding percentage playing every inning at first base.

That’s not quite as succinct as the “below-average fielder” phrasing on his dad’s page. Was Prince also a below-average fielder?

I kind of felt bad sharing that video of Prince Fielder making an error, so here’s a video of him winning the Home Run Derby at the 2012 MLB All-Star Game.

Comparing Cecil’s stats with Prince’s tells an interesting story. While Prince’s career ended prematurely due to a career-ending injury, he played more games than his father, in part because he was playing at an all-star level more or less immediately. (Cecil, on the other hand, spent years paying his dues, including a season in Japan, before his breakout 1990 season with the Tigers.)

Even so, their career fielding percentages ended up fairly similar. Overall, Prince’s fielding percentage was a mere .001 better than his father’s, but setting aside Cecil’s moonlighting at other positions, each had a .992 fielding percentage at first base.

While on the surface Cecil might be a worse fielder, neither were particularly great fielders. In fact, Prince’s range numbers were actually lower than Cecil’s—but as Cecil was more frequently a DH, especially later in his career, you could probably have a good debate over who’s the worse fielder.

Hey Cecil, Prince: Nobody would be mad if you changed your family’s last name to “Slugger.”

The Bittersweet tale of Neversink, New York, the town whose original location ironically became a reservoir

The town of Neversink, New York, up in the Catskills of New York state, is more than 100 miles away from New York City by driving distance, and about 75 as the crow flies. But the ongoing demands of NYC were enough to change its fortunes and ensure that the city would always come up in textbooks about irony.

Throughout the state of New York, ongoing demands to help support the ever-massive needs of New York City led to common cases of eminent domain or condemnation of small towns to make room for reservoirs to support the needs of a massive city. For example, the town of Gilboa, which started as a settlement in 1760 and became an official town in 1848, was flooded in 1926 by the Schoharie Reservoir, a dam built on the Schoharie Creek. The portions of the town that are now literally underwater are called Old Gilboa.

In 1931, a case that went to the Supreme Court essentially gave New York flexibility to divert water from the Delaware River and its tributaries to ensure the city had a strong, continuous water supply. From the summary of :

The diversion from the tributaries of the amount proposed by New York will not materially affect the sanitary condition of the river, its industrial and agricultural uses, its use as a source of municipal water supply, or its shad fisheries. But it is necessary that the diversion should be curtailed and regulated, and be accompanied by sanitary treatment of sewage entering the stream in New York, in order to prevent injury to the use and reputation of the river for recreational purposes in New Jersey, and in order to avoid an increase of salinity in the lower river and in Delaware Bay which would injure the oyster industry there.

The result put small riverside communities like Neversink on blast, allowing the state to more or less move or remove towns that would potentially get in the way of giant dams. In 1941, thanks to a judicially empowered Board of Water Supply, it was decided: The original location of Neversink was condemned, in favor of allowing the state to divert water from the Neversink River for a reservoir that would supply drinking water to one of the largest cities in the world.

And yes, that meant Neversink’s original location, which also dated to the 18th century, was destined to sink. The situation was bittersweet in more ways than one: Quite literally, a neighboring town to Neversink was called Bittersweet, and it was overtaken by the reservoir, too. Unfortunately, it, along with three other communities flooded for nearby reservoir, did not survive the condemnation.

(One of those communities was named Eureka, which is a completely different kind of nominative antideterminism.)

It took many years for the relocation to actually happen, because reservoirs take a long time to build. (A whole World War began and ended in the time between initial proposals and completion.) Moves like these created major challenges for communities similar to Neversink, as noted by a 2016 story on the similarly to-be-sunk towns of Pepacton, Union Grove, Shavertown, and Arena:

Reservoir construction had been underway for two years when a crowd of townspeople gathered at Shavertown’s general store in 1949. Every day the work inched closer to completion, and so did the time they would have to leave the idyllic village where their families had lived for generations. The city of New York would dole out compensation for their homes and relocation, but this was a small comfort to some, who didn’t even know when moving day would arrive.

“We are pushing construction as fast as the weather and the good Lord will permit us,” Irving Hite, president of the Board of Water Supply told the . They hoped to finish the project by 1955 and promised not to “take a single acre of land until it is absolutely necessary.”

Meanwhile, the villages lived on borrowed time; farmers hesitated to plant or expand their herds.

Like those towns, Neversink sank, but it ultimately survived the condemnation by moving its residents to another location nearby. Bittersweet, sadly but fittingly, did not. (Bittersweet was a good example of nominative determinism.)

In its place sits a reservoir that, on a good day, can hold up to 34.9 billion gallons of water, and (via a network of other reservoirs and the Delaware Aqueduct), eventually makes the long trip to New York City, where it ends up in fancy glass water bottles that people may or may not drink when they go to brunch.

That’s the tale of Neversink’s nominatively antideterministic life. On the other hand, Neversink was once nominatively deterministic in a completely different way: It was a dry town for 80 years, including during the period when it was getting flooded and they probably could have used the alcohol. (A hotel that straddled the towns of Montela and Eureka had some, but after the floodings, it suddenly became hard to find.)

When we’re born a thing is created, it’s given a name. We don’t have control over it usually, unless we choose a stage name like David Bowie, or Elton John.

But sometimes it’s entirely possible for a stage name that you decided for yourself to become antideterministic. That brings us to the tale of Johnny Paycheck, which, while directly inspired by a boxer, suggests a person who knows how to make a few bucks here and there. (But to be clear, not Cash. Different guy entirely.)

But Mr. Paycheck’s name—which he legally adopted in the mid-1960s—turned out to be ironic in more ways than one. First, his biggest hit was called “Take This Job and Shove It,” which is literally about a regular paycheck. Later in life, Paycheck, born Donald Eugene Lytle, faced a number of legal and financial troubles and eventually filed for bankruptcy after he failed to pay his taxes.

Nobody has to live up to their name. But it’s fascinating when someone fails to live up to a name that they personally chose for themselves.

items.title: Let’s Deconstruct Photoshop
items.author: Ernie Smith
items.content:
A quixotic new project takes an AI-first approach to battling Adobe, and while it’s unclear where it leads, it raises important questions about what happens when companies ignore their users.

I am not a unique flower. Like many creatives, I had a good relationship with Adobe that, over time, went belly up.

The first sign something was wrong was when the company more or less ignored Mac design conventions in a way that made its software harder to use. (All you had to do was support full-screen apps in Mac OS X Lion, dudes!)

Then it turned its subscription plan into the only real option. Then it kept raising prices. Then it changed its offering in a way that suggested it only really cared about customers who could pay them for hundreds of licenses each year.

On top of that, it failed to keep up with where I was going as a user, along with many other users. Despite the fact that a huge contingent of power users have been decamping to Linux, it more or less ignored those users. Meanwhile, AI changed the definition of what software could be.

That perhaps explains why I’m not particularly surprised that some programmer decided to rebuild the Creative Cloud suite using clean-room techniques in a vibe-coded environment. It solves many of the issues that upset power users—the lack of end-user responsiveness, the high cost, and the ability to use it on the platform of their choice. Adobe, as a public company, has often been tethered to the desires of the stock market, which has meant a lot of AI stuff, even when many creatives have made clear they do not want them.

So now, we have ArtCraft out here Robin Hooding every single one of the key Adobe apps.

Do they work particularly well? On the surface, yes. Opening up these apps in AppImage shows that these apps, programmed in the Rust programming language, are not only fast, but relatively small. Rather than hundreds of megabytes, these apps load in tens of megabytes. They detected my discrete GPU right away. And within a couple of minutes, I was manipulating an image.

A lot of finicky, below the surface stuff did not work so well. Color pickers and secondary menu boxes were rough, not elegant. It did not detect my fonts in DesignCraft until I downloaded an update published just a few minutes before I downloaded it. And while I could set a color with a hex code in PhotoCraft, I could not do the same in DesignCraft.

But it was familiar. I could see myself building a zine with this tool, or using it to access old files that I cannot otherwise open without a Creative Cloud subscription.

Is an open-source vibe-coded creative suite really worth cheering on? I think so.

There are real reasons to cheer on something like this, even if you otherwise hate AI. The spirit of this evokes a Robin Hood-like mindset, in that it exists because of real ethical and economic issues around Adobe that many end users have long been stuck with. In one sense, it is “fighting AI slop with AI slop.” And even if you don’t end up using these tools, the techniques that these projects land on will ultimately inspire open-source projects that actually rely on craft. There are other apps that have emerged in the past couple of years that hope to bring design to Linux; this open-source tool may have opened up a shortcut for these projects.

Let’s talk about “craft” a second here: I think it’s a bad name to build around for this project, as cool and interesting as it is. Craft implies that a lot of heart was put into the code, that it was built by an expert. Which may be true of the artists and creatives that actually use this thing, but does it really speak to what the vibe coders are actually doing? Probably not. It’s really easy to not give critics something to point to, so don’t give it to them.

Another thing that they’re likely to point to is the inherent security issues that might come with a tool like this. The decision to use Rust as the language is likely to help with stability, but it’s not like any regular user is going to be looking at the code here.

But AI coding techniques are likely to change our relationship with open source for good, as seen with the recent AI-based fork of Asahi Linux. And in fact, it may change how companies like Adobe think of open source and vibe coding.

Who knows how legal this is? This feels like one a legit lawyer should probably weigh in on. But some of the language creator Brandon Thomas has used on forums and the ArtCraft website evokes the spirit of Napster, an icon of tech rebelliousness that is not exactly very rebellious in 2026. Napster was not legal, but it still changed everything. That’s a better place for AI in the cultural conversation than “everyone making the worst signs you’ve ever seen.”

And even if ArtCraft’s wild deconstruction project fails, it feels clear others will try to take its place. Which is exactly what happened with Napster.

So the Ellisons own Warner Bros. Discovery, which I don’t love. But you know what I do love? That the anti-animation monster named David Zaslav isn’t in charge anymore.

The fact that a political candidate turned a famous sketch into a very effective political ad is the kind of world I want to live in.

I’m getting sent a lot of single-serving sites at the moment. Here’s one that’s an iPod-themed music game that you might enjoy.

Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal! PhotoCraft, by the way, doesn’t support animated GIFs just yet, but it does have the Save for Web legacy menu, which I was able to use to make today’s header. Not a bad start.

items.title: Missing Link
items.author: Ernie Smith
items.content:
Some spare thoughts about Link, a newspaper that turned 20 years old today—but more or less changed my life. It's been 18 years, but I still miss that job.

As I’ve written in the past, I look longingly at the era of the free daily newspaper. It was an era that represented much of my traditional newspaper career, and it’s one that has been more or less forgotten about by mainstream journalism.

But I had the chance to work at three of them, one of which was among the largest of its kind in the country, the . I loved that paper, though I admit that when I think back to my time in newspapers, I think about above everything else.

, a publication of the that began its life 20 years ago today, started with a provocative idea: What if you could take a 30-column-inch story and condense it into a 3-column-inch story? You could present the information in a new way, leaning on alternative story forms; you could make room for more visuals. And you could inform someone who might not have time for a long-form newspaper in a matter of minutes.

I think fondly of this paper for a number of reasons. To keep in the spirit of the alt-story-form in which it worked:

  1. The format of the newspaper was always a bit like a puzzle to me. We essentially were building a magazine from scratch five days a week, sometimes producing ambitious pages without even knowing what would be on the front page that day.
  2. Though I was a designer, this was the first real experience I got with editing copy, learning the process of taking a story down to the studs and still making it feel dynamic and informative. It taught me a lot about brevity and telling a story through its elements, not just through prose.
  3. It was a strange newsroom by the time it ended; four designers, six copy editors, a web guy, a single reporter, and the editor-in-chief. In most newsrooms, this order would be flipped entirely. But this made room for a ton of ideas, as we took the best of the and presented it to people who would never pick up a copy of the otherwise. (What was also great was that some folks in the main newsroom actually made time for us nerds.)
  4. I had never lived in a community quite like Norfolk, which was small enough to be accessible but large enough that there was always something going on. In terms of real life, it was probably the most social I’ve ever felt living somewhere. I’m actually still in touch with some of the folks I met during this era, both in the newsroom and outside of it.
  5. After this paper shut down, it inspired me to start a blogging career that was driven by this format. I’ve more or less have been doing it ever since, though I write a lot more than I did in 2006.

While this little newspaper had lots of little strengths, there were some weaknesses with the format that perhaps are more obvious from a healthy distance. Most free daily newspapers were intended for commuter-friendly towns, generally to be read on the train or bus. Hampton Roads, alas, is infamously a car-centric community with a number of bridge-tunnels connecting its various parts. Despite being a factor in its creation, the region only got its first light rail system three years Link ended, and that system has yet to get out of Norfolk to any of the numerous other cities in the region.

The other factor, and not an uncommon one with papers of its type: Its internet presence was more or less anemic. (Yes, given the name, somewhat ironic.) Unlike so many newspapers of its era, it didn’t have much of a website, in part out of concern that it would directly compete with the main publication, and in part because the paper effectively was a reformatting of long-form newspaper content in an inventive way.

It ended in the same sad way so many other things ended: As news of the 2008 recession was breaking, we found out layoffs were happening at the , and it was strongly hinted that would be on the chopping block. But it did not shut down right away, but with a two-month delay, with the paper ending just before Christmas, 2008. Unlike Lehman Brothers, we had a proper chance to say a very long goodbye to this job we all loved. (A sign that there might have been some regrets about this shift: About six months after the paper shut down, when I was merely visiting Norfolk, I ran into the business executive in charge of the ’s publishing businesses at a coffee shop, and, seemingly embarrassed to be running into a guy he laid off not that long ago, he sheepishly suggested that he would try to bring this paper back. I’m probably safe to assume it’s not happening at this point.)

Two decades later, I still find myself looking back at this era, with this job that paid more in the form of freedom than it did money, and thinking I had it all figured out. At least some of the glass is rose-tinted, I will admit. But ultimately, set me up for a different kind of success after the 27-month experience of a great job ended. I ended up getting my gig at and moving to D.C., where I immediately met my future wife, and found myself becoming a blogger of modest note. I would sometimes get yelled at for showing up to the paper too early to work, not because I was trying to score overtime, but because I was excited by the work. I eventually put that energy into the digital realm instead.

At this point, I’m pretty much a fully digital creature. But it’s hard to get the ink stains off my fingers all these years later, and while I had the bug before I worked at , it was where it really stuck for me. I still integrate alt-story-form into my various projects, and if I ever find a pocket of time to build it, I still own the domain to the former website, as well as a newspaper box that currently sits in my living room.

Over the past few years, an art collective driven by fans of has been periodically publishing new versions of the newspaper, independently of . I’m probably not doing any of that. While I don’t have a printing press at my disposal, I do have a bunch of old issues, some PDFs, and a brain full of memories. Oh, and the box. And the domain.
